title: First instrument: guitar lessons with Francisco Quinones
summary: Martin's first instrument was guitar, taught by a Mexican bandsman who nicknamed him Chinito and wanted him to learn piano, which scared him off.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Yeah. What was your first instrument then? A guitar or a mandolin?

No, the guitar was my first instrument. The guitar was the very first. Yeah. I had one of the best professors, in fact. Well, that was years ago. You might remember, I don't forgot it was in what city it was, but the Queen's own band from Spain, New Mexico came down here. And he happened to be the baritone player, the brass baritone player. Baritone player. And he was a guitarist. When I say he was a guitarist, he was one of the finest, like that. Well, when the band went back, he stood here. What was his name? Francisco Quinones. Francisco Quinones. That was his name, Francisco Quinones. And I mean, that fellow was, he was out of this world. I seen him not because he was a drinker. He used to love to drink. And I'm telling you, sometimes he'd be just wobbling, staggering over the chair. But you'll never know it by his plan. And of course, he didn't play jazz, I'll admit that. He played nothing but waltzes and tangos naturally. So the standard style of rhythm. And operas and marches and things of that kind and operas. You know what I mean? But he was wonderful. How old were you when you heard him? Oh, gee. That was about when I was around 10, 11 years old. Well, we happened to be living in the same Bowden House at the time. It was a Filipino that was used to run it. It was a restaurant in a Bowden House, you see. Here in New Orleans? Yeah. Right on the ice line between Royal and Charters. Right across the street from Bracato's Ice Cream. Oh, yeah. And well, he started to learn some of the boys are playing and I happened that I was one of them. And he said, well, I got along all right. Until he'd seen that I was progressing pretty fast. And he says, well, now speaking about, now we're going to turn this around, speaking about Jack Lane. Jack Lane gave me the name of Chink Morton. And I always did say that he was the cause of Chink Morton giving me that name that it stuck to me, that he was the first one. But when I come to realize and think about it, it was not. It was this Mexican professor. Oh, he did. In Spanish, he used to call me in place, a call of Martin, which is more than in Spanish. He would call me Chinito. That means China. Oh, yeah. Yeah. The little Chinaman. Yeah. The little Chinaman. Yeah. The little Chinaman. Yeah. See. So he really was the first one that done it, you see. Yeah. Well, anyway, when he said that I progressed so much, you know, and so fast on the guitar, he says, well, now, he says, listen, you're just wasting your talent. On something like this. He says, tell you what I'm going to do. He says, you've got to start to learn. On the next lesson, you're going to start to learn music. And he says, and I want to put you on the guitar. Well, that scared me to death. That was the last time he ever saw me. Oh. I never got around. When he started about, he was going to learn me music and he was going to put me on piano. Because at that time, when you would say piano, it seems to me it was an instrument, which not only to me, to everybody else, it seemed, that it was a girl instrument. That anybody, a man would sit down and play a piano, they'd call him a sissy. Which is the truth. Yeah, I've heard that. That is the truth. You'd sit down and a man sit down and play a piano like that, they'd call him a sissy. Now, that sounds funny, you know, it sounds like, well, that kind of frightened me and I said, no, I'll never make it like that. So that was it.
